stories.headline: Péter Magyar sworn in as Hungary's prime minister, ending Orbán's 16-year rule
stories.summary: Péter Magyar was formally elected prime minister by the new National Assembly on May 9 with 140 votes in favour, 54 against, taking the oath of office in a ceremony laden with pro-EU symbolism including the restoration of the EU flag to the parliament building for the first time since 2014. An estimated 200,000 people gathered on Kossuth Square for post-inauguration celebrations. Magyar pledged 'regime change' and constitutional reform, promising to investigate corruption and restore democratic checks and balances.

stories.headline: Magyar demands President Sulyok and Fidesz-appointed officials resign by May 31; presidential palace responds with brief constitutional rebuff
stories.summary: In his first speech as prime minister, Magyar publicly called on President Tamás Sulyok, the heads of the Constitutional Court, the Supreme Court, and the Prosecution to resign no later than May 31, describing them as 'puppets of the old regime.' Sulyok's office responded tersely, citing the constitution's provisions on presidential tenure; Sulyok nonetheless signed the new government's first two laws the same evening. Political analysts described the confrontation as unprecedented.

stories.headline: Mi Hazánk walks out of inaugural parliamentary session over EU anthem and Roma children's performance, triggering controversy
stories.summary: All six Mi Hazánk MPs left the chamber before the EU anthem 'Ode to Joy' was played and before a Roma children's tamburine ensemble performed at the inaugural session; they also took their parliamentary oaths separately before the Holy Crown. The episode sparked widespread criticism, a public statement from the 100 Tagú Cigányzenekar accusing the party of exclusion, and a counter-claim by Toroczkai that Tisza had broken a prior agreement on the programme order. Mi Hazánk also submitted its first constitutional amendment proposals immediately after the session.

The story attracted extensive international coverage far beyond Hungary.

stories.headline: Fidesz transition to opposition: Orbán skips parliament farewell, Gulyás leads new opposition faction
stories.summary: Viktor Orbán broke 36 years of post-1990 tradition by not attending the inaugural session and delivering no farewell speech, instead giving an interview to rapper Dopeman and updating his Facebook profile to remove his PM title. Fidesz faction leader Gulyás Gergely pledged to operate as a 'normal opposition' while criticising Magyar's tone toward Sulyok. Insider reports indicated Orbán told allies the Fidesz brand may be too damaged to win future elections under its current name.

stories.headline: Magyar's brother-in-law withdraws as justice minister candidate; new justice minister named
stories.summary: Márton Melléthei-Barna, a lawyer married to Magyar's sister, withdrew his candidacy as justice minister after criticism of nepotism, stating he did not want to 'cast the slightest shadow' on the political transition; Magyar defended his credentials before the withdrawal. Görög Márta, a lawyer decorated by the Fidesz government but respected across party lines, was named as the replacement justice minister.

stories.headline: Poland's fugitive ex-justice minister Ziobro flees Hungary to US after Magyar takes office
stories.summary: Zbigniew Ziobro, Poland's former justice minister facing criminal charges in Warsaw, confirmed on Sunday that he had left Hungary for the United States, where he received a visa from the Trump administration. Ziobro had been sheltered in Hungary under Orbán. Magyar had publicly stated before his inauguration that Hungary would no longer protect individuals wanted by allied countries.
